title: 2026 Open Access Week: What Is the Cost of Keeping Knowledge Closed?
content:
Blog post by Clara Riera and Stephen Wyber

When we talk about the cost of scholarly publishing, we tend to focus on subscription bills, publishing fees and the budgets needed to make research Open Access. But these figures tell only part of the story. This year’s Open Access Week theme, “The Cost of Knowledge”, asks us to look further: the cost of closed knowledge also lies in the opportunities lost when those who need it cannot access, share, or reuse research.

A recent European Commission expert report on Open Access policies across EU Member States highlights the challenges. While there is a cost to the activities involved in enabling a well-functioning scholarly communications system (estimated at around 100 000 full-time equivalent staff, of which over half are within research institutions), ways of paying for it that create barriers risk generating their own costs.

title: Buy the Book, Lose the Book: Netherlands’ Market Authority Challenges Bundled Educational Licences
content:
Blog post by Maarten Zeinstra

The Netherlands’ Market Authority (ACM) has warned educational publishers to stop bundling physical book sales with licenses to digital material, effectively making the educational books worthless after one year. The ACM identifies an expected market failure: an uncompetitive market where dominant publishers exploit buyers who do not sufficiently organise themselves. Individual secondary schools lack the power to negotiate fair terms, leaving publishers free to impose restrictive licensing conditions that eliminate the reuse of physical materials.

The case (ACM/25/199621) started in early 2026 with the announcement of a study into educational materials in the Netherlands’ secondary education sector. The ACM had previously received signals in 2024 that this market was not functioning properly, pointing to bundled sales that led to waste of educational material, vendor lock-in, and consumer inertia.
